props.title: Plan 9 from Outer Space
props.initialSlug: Aliens raise zombies to stop Earth from doom

sections.content: Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) stands as the crown jewel of "so-bad-it's-good" cinema, directed by the infamous Ed Wood. Shot on a shoestring budget with recycled footage of Bela Lugosi (who died during production), paper plate flying saucers, and wobbly tombstones, it's a masterclass in accidental comedy. The film's spectacular failures - from the day-to-night continuity errors to actress Vampira's silent screams - created a template for cult movie appreciation that influenced everything from The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) to Troll 2 (1990).

sections.content: The film's legacy extends far beyond its technical shortcomings. Ed Wood (1994) portrayed its creation as a triumph of passion over talent, with Tim Burton celebrating Wood's unwavering optimism. This sparked a revolution in how we view "bad" movies, leading directly to modern celebration of films like The Room (2003) and Birdemic: Shock and Terror (2010). Plan 9's influence can be seen in deliberate B-movies like Mars Attacks! (1996), which pays homage to Wood's earnest alien invasion narrative.

The film's aliens-raising-the-dead plot, while nonsensical, actually preceded George Romero's Night of the Living Dead (1968) by nearly a decade. Its blend of science fiction and horror, however unintentionally, helped establish tropes that would become genre staples. Modern filmmakers like James Gunn have cited Plan 9's earnest weirdness as inspiration, visible in works like Slither (2006). SUBHEAD: The Cultural Impact of "Bad" Movies

movies.title: Mystery Science Theater 3000: The Movie
movies.slug: The ultimate celebration of bad movie viewing culture, showing how films like Plan 9 should be watched.

sections.content: Plan 9's elevation to cult status helped establish the midnight movie circuit that would later champion films like Pink Flamingos (1972) and Eraserhead (1977). Its reputation grew through late-night TV screenings, creating a shared cultural experience of collective appreciation for cinematic failure. This phenomenon continues today through platforms like RiffTrax and bad movie podcasts, all tracing their DNA back to Wood's magnum opus.
